utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, we are prepared to call our first witness, Fejzija Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting to bring the witness into the courtroom, I can advise you that based on the Trial Court's ruling on the adjudicated facts, the Prosecution does not intend to lead evidence that has been covered extensively through adjudicated fact 731 through 746.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Mladic consults with counsel, if he takes off his earphones, then there's no need to speak as loudly as he does, because that disturbs, to some extent, the order in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hadzic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic. Please be seated. Mr. Hadzic, I do not know what you are putting on your table, but if you want to consult any piece of paper, then please ask for permission first. You'll now be examined by Ms. Bibles. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And to answer the Court's questions, I believe the witness was retrieving his eyeglasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's very good. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't see it from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I am Fejzija Hadzic, born on the 1st of January, 1947. My father's name is Fejzo, my mother's name is Asaja, and I was born near Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And which village in Kalinovik did you live in before the war?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Mjehovina Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you have provided witness statements to the Bosnian authorities and to ICTY regarding your experiences during the war?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, could I ask that page 1 of 65 ter 28354 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As to the statements, have you had an opportunity to review the statement you made to the Bosnian authorities in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have such an opportunity. And the statement does reflect what you said, and the signature on the statement is mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at the screen and specifically looking at the handwritten document. Do you recognise this document based on your view of this page?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do recognise this document. I read it. I looked through it, and I signed it my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: This is a statement that I gave in 1992 to the Bosnian authorities, to the centre for investigating war crimes and genocide against the Muslims in Zenica. I testified about what happened while I was in camp --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Was this a statement that you gave on the 20th of October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could we now turn to the last page of the document. I believe it's page 4 on the B/C/S version. Could you look at this page and tell us whether you recognise your signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is the information contained in this statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we were to ask you about the matters contained in this statement today, would your answers today be the same as they were in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the first page of 65 ter 28353 please be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You also provided a statement to ICTY?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review the statement that you gave to ICTY?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have an opportunity to review it, and I noticed that there's a mistake. Instead of the 31st of January, 1991, it should say 31st of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And is this the document that you're looking at, at the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And if we could now go to page 6 in both versions of this document. Do you recognise your signature on this -- on the last page of this document?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, in fact, did you sign or initial every page of this statement?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Aside from the date of -- on the first page, is this statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of both statements?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28353 and 28354 for admission, pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Madam Registrar, 28353 ICTY witness statement, 31st of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 28353 becomes Exhibit P138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P138 is admitted into evidence. Then the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28354 becomes Exhibit P139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P139 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, with your leave, I'll slowly review a brief summary of Mr. Hadzic's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've explained to Mr. Hadzic what the purpose of it is?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Mr. Hadzic has said, he is from Kalinovik municipality which he explains in this statement is also the home municipality of the accused, Ratko Mladic. Mr. Hadzic is a Muslim and as the war started he was the director of the public utilities company for Kalinovik. Despite the assurances for safety that was given to the Muslim community and Mr. Hadzic during the time that the ethnic cleansing began, Mr. Hadzic and other Muslim men from the municipality were arrested on or around the 25th of June, 1992. They were first held in the elementary school in town, and then, on the 6th of July, they were moved to an ammunition warehouse. They were held there through and until the first part of August 1992. During the first weeks of August 1992, groups of Muslim detainees were taken out from the detention facility and many were not seen again. On the 5th of August, 1992, Mr. Hadzic, along with 23 other Muslim men, were taken from the facility. They were beaten. Mr. Hadzic's hands were bound with wire and their valuables were taken from them. Mr. Hadzic, along with the others, were lined up and shot as a group. The bodies who had been shot, including Mr. Hadzic, were moved to a stable and lit on fire. Mr. Hadzic, although badly injured, managed to survive and escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you describe that life became intolerable in Kalinovik as a result of a campaign of Serb intimidation. You describe that a group of Chetniks came to the area. Was -- were they part of this intimidation campaign?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, it's always good to know exactly where the summary ends.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the disciplinary is not evidence, and then you move to the examination of the witness. So you have now started questioning the witness just to be clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm sorry. I will clarify for the record I have now completed the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you describe for us the group of Chetniks that came to your area in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: On that day, I was at work. At some point in the afternoon, a large group of Chetniks arrived from Mjehovina led by Pero Elez. They started yelling all about town and shooting and so on. Since we are only about ten minutes away from Kalinovik, there is only a hill between us, I went home so that we could leave the village. In the earlier evening, Grujo Lalovic, the president of the municipal Executive Council and president of the Crisis Staff and of the SDS, he addressed us, and he guaranteed our personal safety and the safety of our property. He said that nothing would happen to us, that they exercise their own influence, that the Chetniks left Kalinovik and that this would not happen again. And he insisted that they be given guarantees from Vucurevic from Trebinje, because it became part of Trebinje through a unilateral decision in 1991. Now that I'm talking about all of these meetings, may I tell you a few more things --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, if we could stop for a second, I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I also ask you to slow down your speed of speech so that the interpreters are able to follow. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I want to go back and ask some very specific questions. You described that the group of Chetniks were led by Pero Elez?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When did they come -- what date did they come to Kalinovik the first time?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: It was the 5th or 6th of May. I cannot tell you exactly. They came in smaller groups even before that, but they did not behave the way they did on that day, on that 5th or 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, is this the same Pero Elez who you saw on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: This was the same group that came and took you away on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: That is what I assume, because they were headed by Pero Elez that is why I assume that all of them were his men.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you tell us during this time-period in -- between May and June of 1992, were there particular Muslims for your community who would meet with different people about this issue of safety?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were meetings. And I wanted to tell you about that. There was this meeting towards the end of April that was also organised by Grujo Lalovic and the commander of the tactical group, Colonel Ratko Bundalo who invited all the representatives of Muslim villages to a meeting at the municipal hall and he presented to us the following: He said that we should not be afraid because even before that --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Even before that, we had addressed the municipal assembly asking them to allow us to leave voluntarily. Again, they tried to reassure us to provide security guarantees to us but at this meeting they said that most probably after that meeting, we, all the Muslims, all the Bosniaks, that is, young ones would have to report to the police station in order to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, to go forward in time, could you tell us the names of the Muslims in your community who would meet with the Serbs on behalf of the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: It was Tahir Panjeta and Sacko Keso. I cannot recall all the names of the people from all the villages who attended the meeting at the municipality that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: But they would have been the individuals who met with the Serb leadership periodically, representing the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention now to battery-level weapons which were pointed at a Muslim village in May of 1992. In your statement, you describe that members of the Muslim community complained directly to Ratko Mladic about these weapons. Can you tell us where Ratko Mladic was when that discussion took place?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, look. The next day after that meeting, between Ratko Mladic and the representatives of Golubici, well, Ratko's relatives from that village worked in my company, in the company that I worked in, that is, and they told me that that day Ratko Mladic and Velibor Ostojic arrived by helicopter and they called upon the Muslims of Golubici to discuss the situation and to reach some kind of agreement, and the Muslims complained about these batteries being pointed at Golubici and that is what they minded. The next day, this weaponry was removed and soon after that these artillery weapons were returned to the very same positions and pointed at the village of Golubici, and this village of Golubici was shelled, and Bovice as well in August, and in August it was torched as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Going back to the meeting that the villagers had with General Mladic, are you familiar with the message that Ratko Mladic had for the villagers on that day in May?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was. He said to them that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be a Serb state and that the laws of this Serb state had to be observed in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I would like to turn your attention now to the mosques of Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I note we have adjudicated fact 746.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you're aware of who destroyed the four mosques in Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: All four mosques in Kalinovik were used before the war except for one of them, the one in Velisi [phoen]. From 1991 to 1995 all three mosques in the territory of the municipality of Kalinovik were torched. The minaret was blown up and the one in the village --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the village. The name of the village --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the one in the neighbouring village was also destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One minute, Mr. Hadzic. The question and I would like you to focus your answers on what is asked is: Who destroyed the four mosques. Not about how they were destroyed, but who did it. Whether you have any knowledge about that. Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an answer. It was done by the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I next want to turn to your time when you were detained in the Kalinovik elementary school and then in the ammunition warehouse. Could you tell us the ethnicity of the guards who kept you in those detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: At both places, all the guards were of Serb ethnicity. All of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did the guards wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, olive-green-grey uniforms, military uniforms. And also long-barrelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I want you to think in your mind to the first few days of August of 1992. During that time-period while you were in the warehouse, did you hear automatic gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you describe for us whether you know which day in August this was?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: It was the 1st of August. It was a Saturday, when, in the evening, the village of Jarise [phoen] and the Karaula hamlet were torched and when all the Muslim people from this village were taken away and detained at the Kalinovik elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I now want you to think about the day of the 5th of August, 1992. The men who came to take you away, can you tell us how many were in that group?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: This is a day that was very difficult and that I do not like to remember. Pero Elez and Milenko Fukovic, nicknamed Njeko [phoen], and also a man named Vukadin [phoen], who was our guard, they walked in, they called out the names of 12 prisoners and told them to go out. There were about three or four of them. They wore camouflage uniforms. After that, they took these 12 men away. After a while they returned yet again. Again, they took three men out. They called out their names and they said to the rest of us that we should get ready to go to the KP Dom Foca for an exchange. We actually believed them. We packed some of the things that we had with us and then they came back again and told us that we couldn't take anything along, and they said that a group of young men would have their hands tied so that they could not escape. Then they started tying their hands. Then it came to be my turn. They used a wire to tie my hands and they told us to go out. As we were leaving the building, I was hit badly by a wooden stick -- with a wooden stick and then we got into a TAM 110 vehicle, a uniformed soldier was with us who said that we were going to Foca and that we would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, if I can stop you for just a moment. Could you describe for us -- you've said it was a TAM 110 vehicle. Could you describe for us whether that was a civilian vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Military vehicle and military drivers. All the drivers who drove the vehicles wore military uniforms. There was one just civilian vehicle driven by a Muslim. He was the first one so that if the road had been mined, he would be the one to be blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you've said this is a difficult day to remember. I would like to take you towards the end of that day and direct your attention to a couple of questions. When the shooting started against you and the group of men that you were with, what types of weapons were used?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Automatic weapons, automatic rifles. There were bursts of gun-fire fired at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: There were about five or six uniformed soldiers to our left, since we all stood one by one in a line, one after another, and they were there, they shot us. I pretended to be dead but I was just wounded. Before that, they took out four members of the Suljic family. They tied our hands and ordered them to throw us into a barn. They threw me in there as well. I tried to seek shelter so that I wouldn't be covered by all the dead bodies, but then they killed those three men as well. And then they wanted to set fire to all of us, and I saw the fourth Suljic killed by a burst of gun-fire and then they poured gasoline all over and set fire to it. When I heard that there were vehicles there, two more truck-loads of prisoners, that they continued, I managed to run out. Although I had been wounded in the leg, I managed to run out and I fell into a brook. I don't know how long I lay there, and I managed to cut the wire somehow and I tried to save myself and I moved away. And I knew that in Huse there were Muslim refugees. I walked all day and finally joined the other refugees. That is where I was given first aid. And afterwards, I ultimately met up with my family and continued my own life, traumatised as I am to this very day after all these things that happened to me. Let's me just explain this. After that, we met another man. I assume he is Adem Hadzic. They killed him as well. So there were 24 bodies in that barn that were burned and no remains can be found, because in 1999 exhumations were carried out and bones were found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. Of course, you are telling us a lot about what we have read already in your statement. Ms. Bibles put some additional questions to you. The last one was who was doing the shooting. Now, you told us by far more. Could you please focus on what Ms. Bibles asks you. And, Ms. Bibles, could you please -- if the witness strays away from your question. Because much of what you told us, of course, we have read that, and the summary has been read already to the public, and we want to hear as much evidence as possible. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The men who were murdered on the 5th of August, are those men named in the statement that you gave to the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that would be on pages 3 and 4 of the English version of P139. And Your Honours I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you sit down, Madam Bibles, can I just ask a question. Was your question answered as to who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, I believe he testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We were told that these were about five or six uniformed soldiers. I thought when you said "who" you probably were asking for names, if they were known.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I can clarify that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, did you know any of the men who were doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't know any of the men who were doing the shooting. We only knew Pero Elez who was with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Who is it that is going to cross-examine? Mr. Stojanovic, will it be you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic will now cross-examine you. Mr. Stojanovic, you'll find him to your left, is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, any indication as far as the time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already consulted my learned friend, and I announced that my cross-examination will last some 40 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm Miodrag Stojanovic. I come from Bosnia and Herzegovina, just like you. My impression is that both you and I speak very fast, therefore I am going to ask you to slow down a little for the sake of the interpretation. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will then do the same, Mr. Stojanovic, I take it, because you said you're both quick speakers, so your both slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, before I start putting my questions to you. On behalf of Mr. Mladic's Defence team, it is my duty to express my sincere regret for everything that you experienced, for your traumas that you have just told us about and mentioned in your statements. Allow me now to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Trial Chamber if you ever served in the army, and if you did where was that?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spent 18 months in Slovenia in Postojna. I was a communications guy in the anti-aircraft artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us when was that and who was the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: It was in 1966 and 1967. The battery commander was Simo [indiscernible], a captain. I can't tell you more than that after such a long time. And after that, he was replaced by a Macedonian, Lazo Dukovski [phoen], who was also a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this because I realised that you had training in artillery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in anti-aircraft artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When war broke out, you were in Kalinovik. You were the CEO of the local public utility company; right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, were you politically engaged?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to meet Ratko Mladic when you were younger, at school or as an adolescent?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I remember him vaguely as a child when he played football in Pofalici. After that, after elementary school, he went for further education. I stayed in Kalinovik. We saw each other from time to time just in passing. I would say that I -- I know him just from passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that before the war you never heard anything bad about Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the summer of 1992, and that's when the tragic events happened, as you told us, you personally did not have an occasion to see Mr. Mladic; are you [as interpreted] right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The information that you received about the conversations that Mr. Mladic held with the villagers of Golubic is second-hand information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the names of the person from whom he heard information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, could you repeat the names of the two people from whom you received the information, but slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Marko Mladic and Cedo Coso who were employees at my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what the two of them told you, the request of the villagers of Golubici was to remove the -- or, rather, to change the direction of the artillery, which faced the village of Golubici?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't to change the direction but to remove the battery from that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was done; right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But only temporary, for a few days, for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something that I learned while I was preparing for this case and I couldn't find that in any of the statements used in this courtroom. That's why I want to ask you whether it is correct that at one point you were brought to the public security station in Kalinovik in the year 1992 because they wanted to check a suspicion according to which you were one of the organisers of the Bosniak population resistance?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that did happen. I went there. I spent a couple of hours at the public security station where I was interviewed and then I was released and I continued working. I have to say that I never participated in the organisation of any resistance. If that had been the case, I would not have stayed in Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was established that the suspicions were -- were unfounded and false?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I continued working.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you continued working in your company?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 25th of June, 1992, and you understand why I mentioned that date, you were not militarily engaged; right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, if I'm not mistaken, if -- and if I studied the documentation well, you were given work obligation and then you were arrested by the police officers from Kalinovik; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we all reported to the Secretariat for National Defence for work obligation we were surrounded by the reserve and active-duty police officers. They loaded us onto cars and arrested us, and after that a lot more people were brought from their homes so that that evening there were about 60 of us in the elementary school in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that according to your best recollection the police officers who were present when you were arrested and when you were brought to the elementary school and whom you remembered were Milan Peric and Saso Doder?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. They arrived in a TAM 110. Peric parked the car and Doder orders us to get into the car. Gojko Lalovic, the chief of the civilian protection imposed that. He insisted that a meeting should be held and that we should not be arrested. However, this must have been prearranged. We had to be called to the [indiscernible] and that was the motive for our arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please. Let's slow down. Please. The police officers and the cars that you mentioned, they took you to the elementary school in Kalinovik; right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And there you were taken over by some other police officers and they were the ones who searched all of you who had been brought in?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: There must have been some 10 or 15 reserve police officers who took turns. They worked in shift as they guarded us in the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your statements and your testimony in other cases, you remember that among those police officers, the employees of the police station in Kalinovik, were Aleksandar Cerovina, Predo Terzic and Dusko Mandic; right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I remember that those were the men who searched us at the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the elementary school -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: When they loaded us on to the car and when they brought us to the school, they were the ones who searched us at the entrance of the gym and they took any sharp objects from us. Those three. The others guarded us. That's why I'm saying that at least 10 or 15 reserve police officers were engaged in the guard duty, but they worked in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. This is precisely what I wanted to hear from you. Those persons, those individuals who guarded you, were also police officers; right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were reserve policemen. All that happened at the elementary school. They were other persons in the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A few days later, the police officers whom you have mentioned transferred you to the depot which had been transformed?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Let me put it that way. Yes, on that day, three military cars arrived and stopped in front of the elementary school. There was some uniformed people in the cars, and the reserve police officers escorted us to the depot where we were taken over by active-duty officers in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's stop here and let's clarify one or two things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, active-duty officers. Were they still police officers or were they army officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Active police officers who served in Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for the assistance. I will go along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the depot, according to your best recollection, somebody was there and introduced himself to you as the officer serving at that facility --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the counsel please repeat the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the name, Mr. Stojanovic, you just mentioned, the officer that introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat slowly and then I will ask you about that man. The person who was there waiting for you who was in charge of the depot, according to him, was Djordje Slavaskraba [as interpreted]; right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe I should spell the name because it seems that the name has not been recorded properly. I agree, it's a bit unusual. With your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. You don't need permission to do that. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A-s-k-r-a-b-a D-o-r-d-i-s-l-a-v. I hope this was of some assistance to everybody. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you check on the transcript that it's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have checked. Yes, it's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you know the man from before?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I knew Djordje Askraba from before because for a while, he was a police officer in Kalinovik and a few years before the war, he was transferred to Sarajevo. He was retired then. I know his wife who hails from the same village. There is a relationship between my father-in-law and his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that he is Grujo's son?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And that he is about your age?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, I would kindly ask you to confirm that, to your best recollection, he was also a police officer?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a retired policeman. And at that facility he guarded us not wearing a police uniform but a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's -- let me now direct your attention to the time that you spent at that facility. Please bear with me, Your Honours. To your best recollection, how many rooms were there where you were accommodated at the depot?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: We were in a large room. Before the war, it was a store room for explosives of the Yugoslav People's Army. It was about 10 to 16 metres long, and on three sides, there were wooden pallets on the concrete floor. We did not have any beds or bedding. We had to sleep on those wooden pallets on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at one point in time it was possible for you, it was made possible for you to visit your family and for blankets to be provided to you to make it easier for you?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the second day, the following day when we could meet our families, but it had been forbidden in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, your question was translated as whether it was made possible for the witness to visit his family. Is it for the witness to visit his family or for the family to visit the witness? What exactly was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I saw those lines. They are lines 16 and 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And my question was: Did they allow your families to visit you in that facility?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our families, all the families, visited us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This has been clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Having been in that gun powder depot for several days, do you have the opportunity of meeting Mr. Askraba?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every day -- in fact, we weren't there for over a few days. We spent over 30 days in that facility. We met Djordje Askraba who always told us that he was responsible for everything and that we should contact him if we needed something. The guards in military uniforms would contact him. It was possible he would provide us with some food. If not, nothing happened. During those 30 days, nothing much was delivered to the gun powder depot, nothing much apart from these blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The guards in the depot, did you know them?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew all of them, apart from two men from Sarajevo and two from Foca. I knew everyone else because I had worked and co-operated with them. I had socialised with them. But while I was in the camp, they no longer knew me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, were you in a position to get to know the person you called Mr. Bundalo in the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that I ever stated that I saw Mr. Bundalo in the depot because we only saw the person who introduced himself as the assistant commander for security, but I don't remember Ratko Bundalo ever appearing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a good opportunity for me to ask you to tell the Court whether you know what sort of the duties at the time Mr. Bundalo performed?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: When I was a free man, I know that he was the local commander because he had come from Rijeka. Rade Pavlovic was replaced. He was the commander of the military -- 27 -- 27 up until that point in time and Ratko Bundalo, who was either a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel at the time, replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the person you have called Ratko Bundalo is not from Kalinovik, he wasn't born there, and he didn't previously live there?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No, the first time I heard of him was when he returned to the camp and there were problems with the water supply and that's when I heard him introduce himself as the commander. That's when I came to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which specific military unit he was a member of?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the Kalinovik group. I don't know what it's called. I wouldn't go into those establishment details. I know that he was the commander for places called Trnovo, Kalinovik and Foca. Because that's why the local Bosnian authorities sentenced him to 21 years in prison, in fact. It was on the basis of that position that he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So that is, in fact, the question I want to put to you. It has to do with that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, perhaps this would be a good time to have a break, because I will be moving onto certain questions that are related to the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how much time would you need after the break, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, Your Honours, I believe that I will need the same amount of time that I have already used up to complete my cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be close to one hour. I think you said you need 40 minutes, which is an extension of 20 minutes. Apart from that, approximately 60 or 70 per cent of your questions are just seeking confirmation of what is already either in the statement of the witness or what he testified during examination-in-chief. So would you please try to focus on what really is needed in cross-examination, and I'll consult with my colleagues how much time you have for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber expects you to use not more than 20 minutes after the break. And please focus on matters in dispute and matters of relevance and importance. We -- I would first like to have the witness escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes. Mr. Hadzic, could you follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber establishes that Mr. Mladic did not -- is not in the courtroom at this moment. Mr. Stojanovic, we were informed that Mr. Mladic reported not to feel well. Could you update the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. We have just left the room in which we were with Mr. Mladic, and we tried to deal with the issue, and Mr. Mladic was very upset. He was red in the face. He was very excited. And my colleague, Mr. Ivetic, has remained with him, but I entered the courtroom as the trial was scheduled to commence again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if someone doesn't appear in court, a few questions arise. The first one is whether he waives his right to be present. It's simply either you do or you do not. Then the second issue, if he waives his right to be present, we could finish the last 20 minutes of this witness and then reconsider the matter, because we then have to take a break anyhow for the preparation of the protective measures for the next witness. So that's the first issue: Waiver, yes or no. Second issue. If Mr. Mladic would not waive his right to be present, then in order not to continue the proceedings, a medical condition should be established which disenables him to be present in court. This Chamber has had some experiences over the last few months with Mr. Mladic reporting that he felt unable to be in court, which was not always confirmed at a later stage by medical reports which said that he really wasn't. So we will be rather strict on that. But the first question is - and I'd like you to raise that, and if you need a few minutes for that, we'll take a short break - whether Mr. Mladic would waive his right, to start with, for the next 20 minutes to finish the cross-examination and perhaps re-examination of the witness, Mr. Hadzic. Could you try to find out?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I'm informing you that when I left the room in which I was, together with Mr. Mladic, he didn't waive that right. He made certain suggestions with regard to the end of the cross-examination of this witness, and if I am to tell you whether anything has changed in the meantime, I would have to go back and see what sort of state Mr. Mladic is in. All I have done is convey my impression of the situation to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that he didn't waive his right is -- doesn't mean that he finally will decide not to waive his right. You said he made certain suggestions with regard to the end of the cross-examination of this witness. Of course, if they are within the realm of client/counsel privilege, you shouldn't say anything about it. If, however, they are of a more practical nature, the Chamber would like to be informed about what these suggestions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. This is confidential information and has to do with the client/counsel privilege. It has to do with the further cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that Mr. Mladic was able to give instructions as to the last part of the cross-examination of this witness. We'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To allow you to take instructions, as far as waiver is concerned, Mr. Stojanovic, we'll take a break for three minutes. --- Break taken at 11.02 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber establishes that Mr. Mladic is in the courtroom. Could the witness be brought in. Mr. Stojanovic, once the witness is -- has entered the courtroom, you have your 20 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his cross-examination. Listen carefully to his questions. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is my cue. You remembered -- you also mentioned trials before the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina when we started.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that in several cases before the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina you testified in relation to all of these things that happened?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you confirm to the Court that you appeared as a witness in relation to these events in the case of Ratko Bundalo?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: And Nedjo Zeljaja and Dragan Savic from Trebinje. All of this had to do with what happened in Kalinovik, Djordje Askraba and the policemen, Peric, Doder and Terzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but let's do this one step at a time so that we deal with it properly.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You testified in the case against Nedjo Zeljaja who at that time was commander of the police station in Kalinovik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Final judgement was passed in relation to these events?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ratko Bundalo, you also testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also to make a pause between answer and question and question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also testified in the case against Ratko Bundalo and he was also convicted and that decision was final?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also testified in the case against Dordislav Askraba and he was also convicted -- I understand.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did testify in Askraba's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in the case against Krsto Savic as well?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As a high police official, he was convicted for all of these things that had happened.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also testified in the case against the policemen that you mentioned today?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is, Milan Peric, Spasoje Doder, Predrag Terzic and Aleksandar Cerovina.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, I did testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these persons were acquitted?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not going to put any other questions in relation to that then. Now, I'm going to move on to what happened on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, just for my understanding of your line of questioning, if you ask a witness whether he testified in other cases and whether those persons were acquitted, what is it the Chamber is supposed to conclude from that or to think about that? Do we have to understand that they may have been acquitted on the basis of the testimony of this witness, or that there may have been other evidence? What are we supposed to do with the answers the witness just gave to your questions? Or is it a suggestion that there's something wrong with the witness's testimony because these people were acquitted? Is that your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. With all due respect, that is exactly what our aim is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it is not dealt with in a proper way. Then you should provide us with testimony of the witness. The only thing I want to say is that the way in which you approached this matter does not give any ground whatsoever for the suggestion you make and is even, to some extent, unfair to the witness. Please be aware of that and continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we shall do our best to call these witnesses and to bring them into this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I am going to ask you something else. You mentioned the people who put you onto these vehicles, and the explanation provided was that you were being taken to the KP Dom Foca; namely, Elez, Pero and Milenko Vukovic, nicknamed Zeko?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, if I may I'd like to go back to those previous questions. I would not agree that they had all been acquitted. On the basis of my testimony was Peric and Doder only, and the rest were found guilty. Because it seemed here that they had all been acquitted on the basis of what I testified about but they were sentenced to a variety of different prison sentences amounting to 71 years in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if Mr. Stojanovic wants to further address the matter, we'll hear that and then preferably in an appropriate manner, and otherwise he will proceed on other subjects. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that these persons came from Mjehovina?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court how far away Mjehovina is from Kalinovik and your village?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I cannot be very specific but it must be about 15 or 16 kilometres between Kalinovik and Miljevina and then since there is a kilometre from Kalinovik to my village, then it is roughly 16 kilometres altogether; that is it my assessment, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that Miljevina does not belong to the municipality of Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Miljevina belongs to the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at that point in time, there was a great deal of fighting at the Rogoj pass and many members of the VRS lost their lives there?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I heard stories to that effect once I got out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serb soldiers were killed then?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. But, look, this is what you're trying to link up. The loss of life by a soldier on the front line and -- is one thing and killing a civilian is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you is the following: The men who were there just before the execution, did they mention what had happened in Rogoj?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. Just one evening, Zdravko Visnjevac came and told us that, that some people had killed -- had been killed at Rogoj and that all of us would be killed. And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber on the basis of the information that you received subsequently when did these things happen at Rogoj?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in addition to the names that you mentioned, did you know who the people who participated in this execution were? Were they soldiers? Were they civilians? Were they policemen?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: We were guarded by soldiers and taken out by soldiers, and there was a police vehicle escorting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: One of these persons introduced himself as a Chetnik from Niksic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he was from Niksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will we agree that Niksic is in Montenegro, that it's not in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And he also said that they were mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, what he said that is, could you conclude on the basis of anything else that these persons came from Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No. As for the dialect, the way they spoke and when they were asking us to sing different songs, the dialect that they used when speaking was not Montenegrin, it was our Bosnian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a name, Tomo Visnjevac. And you said that he spoke about Rogoj.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: It's not Tomo. It's Zdravko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Zdravko Visnjevac. Do you know a name by the name of Todo Visnjevac?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I know him from Kalinovik. He was a driver at the Kalinovik health centre. And it was Zdravko Visnjevac, nicknamed Sjena, who told us in camp that we would be all be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was a member of the military or the police?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: When I was free, I saw him wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you start giving a good example, then perhaps the witness will follow. Can we take it again from -- I think you asked whether he was a member of the military police. And then a part is missing. Was there anything more specific in your question, Mr. Stojanovic? Is that what you asked: "Do you know if he was a member of the military police."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It was "military or police" but it is too fast for the court reporters as well to record all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, due to your speed of speech parts are missing. I do understand now from the interpreters that your question was: "Do you know if he was a member of the military or the police." And the answer of the witness then was: "When I was free, I saw him wearing a military uniform. " If that reflects question and answer, then you now may proceed, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I would like to finish with the questions that I have just received, going back to the part of your proofing that has to do with the arrival of Mr. Mladic. Were you told where it was that Mr. Mladic landed in a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Bozanovici. Above their houses and the cemetery there, there's a big meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know and were you told at whose initiative this meeting took place with the locals from Golubici?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I was not told. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Mladic took one of the locals there from Golubici into the helicopter so that he could see the area?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was told as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And that, on that occasion, he promised him that their request for moving the artillery out would be honoured?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they told us and that's the way it was for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us if you know who this person was who was in the helicopter with Mr. Mladic then?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I don't remember his name. I know he is from Golubici, but I cannot say whether it is this or that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Milan Mandic?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: Milan Mandic? There are several Milan Mandics in Kalinovik, so I cannot say which Milan this would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to conclude by putting a question that has to do with your attitude towards the Mladic family. You said that in relation to all your trials and tribulations, you said that you did not have an opportunity of seeing any of the members of the Mladic family?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I mean, there is the Mladic family, I mean, there's also Lalovics and other families that are related to them. But there was not a single one with the last name of Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not have an opportunity of hearing from anyone that any of the members of the inner circle of the Mladic family appeared in relation to the events that you are testifying about here?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I just know that he was a member of that army, Dusko Mladic. I did not see him. But he did draw on Mr. Ratko's merits and he sort of figured prominently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you did not see this person at any point in time when all of this happened?

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for your testimony. Also, Mr. Mladic told me to say to you that he is prepared to shake hands with you to offer you his hand at any point in time and to apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, offers for restoring relationships are not part and are not part and parcel of cross-examination of a witness. So this is best dealt with, I would say, out of court, not here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I do understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And thank you to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: FEJZIJA HADZIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since the Chamber has no questions for you either, Mr. Hadzic, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and you are excused. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for the fair attitude towards me as a witness. I thank everybody: The Trial Chamber, the Defence, and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I earlier said that we would need a break for protective measures for the next witness, I might have been mistaken because the order of the Prosecution witnesses has changed quite recently, I do understand. It is my understanding that Witness RM010 is the next one on your list. Any need for protective measures? Because, until now, I don't think that we received any request for protective measures. Or are there any existing protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that witness will be taken by Ms. Silvia D'Ascoli which I take the opportunity to introduce to the Chamber. I'll let her address you on the status of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. D'Ascoli, welcome into the court. Protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, pseudonym, voice and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are these protective measures deriving from other cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, from the Krajisnik case. That was the first proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take a break, because, especially voice distortion takes a while to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you tell us how much time would be needed? We could take this as a second break. We might need another one anyhow.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We would need at least 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes. Then I suggest that we resume at a quarter to 12.00 and that we take another 20-minute break before we adjourn at 2.15. We adjourn until 11.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, first of all, apologies that the Chamber was, due to internal malcommunication, unfamiliar with the protective measures, but it's clear. The Prosecution always has presented in the appropriate way. Are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls RM010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: RM010 could be escorted into the courtroom. But I think we need to have the curtains down first because of face and voice distortion. May I emphasise that the parties, whenever any question or answer is at risk to reveal the identity of the witness, that they should ask for private session in order to give proper effect to the protective measures ordered in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and, further, everyone is urged to switch off his own microphones when the witness answers the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime while the witness is brought in, maybe I could indicate to the Chamber the adjudicated facts that the Prosecution will be relying upon for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness RM010. We'll wait first so that the blinds can be up. Meanwhile, I inform you that before giving evidence you are required to make a solemn declaration, of which the text will be handed out to you by the usher. If you wait for a second until the blinds are up ... Yes. May I invite you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness RM010. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM010, your testimony is given under protective measures. No one out of this courtroom will see your face, no one will hear your own voice, and we'll not use your own name but will call you Witness RM010. If there would be any question which you think, if answered in accordance with the truth, would reveal your identity, do not hesitate to ask me to go into private session. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now first be examined by Ms. D'Ascoli. Ms. D'Ascoli is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I will begin by showing you a document which contains some information related to you. Could I please have the pseudonym sheet which is 65 ter number 28355. Sir, please look at the information on the screen but do not read aloud any of the information you see. Can you confirm that this is your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this exhibit -- this 65 ter number into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28355 becomes Exhibit P140, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P140 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us which was the size and the ethnicity of your village?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: The village had about 800 houses and about 75 to 80 per cent were Muslims, and the rest were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us how the relations were between the different ethnicity in your village in the time-period before the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: There were no differences among the two ethnic ethnicities. We went to school together. We socialised together. We shared our lives. We lived next to each other. There were never any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can you tell us if this changed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: Yes. The first obvious changes could be seen in 1991. However, during 1992, those differences intensified in late March and the beginning of April. Things came to a head at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can you describe how the situation in your village was in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: In the month of March, tensions were not as pronounced. However, check-points started being set up on the hills. They were manned by the local Serbs. There were three or four such locations where the Serbs had their observation posts from which they observed what was going on in our village. My village is in a valley, so, from those observation posts, they could observe our movements, where we went, and what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, you said that check-points started being set up on the hills. Do you remember the exact locations, the names of the location, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: Yes. From my house, I could see one of those observation posts at Gologlovo, and on the other side, across the valley from my house, there was another observation point, at Ljunjovo [phoen]. There were a couple more such observation posts that I could not see from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And you said that Serbs were manning these check-points. Can you be more specific? Or can you describe who the Serbs were?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: They were exclusively Serbs. In 1993, they were locals, together with the reservists of the then-army. So those posts were manned by a mixed composition of civilians and soldiers. Those soldiers would go to the front line from time to time, and then, when they returned home, they would be put in charge of manning those observation posts, together with the local civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Let's move to May 1992. Can you tell us whether there were any changes in the situation in your village?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: At the beginning of May, and even before, in the direction of Sanica on the bridge there was a check-point manned by the reserve forces of the police and active-duty policemen. From that check-point, they controlled the entry and exit from Sanica. At the end of May, after the 25th of May, the Muslims who were members of the reserve police were returned from the police station in Sanica because they had not accepted to sign the so-called loyalty oath to the then-police force. On that day, on the 20th [as interpreted] May, a flag of the -- the Republika Srpska was hoisted on the building of the police. They didn't sign that document. They had to return their weapons and uniforms, and they had to go home. From that day on, only the reserve and active-duty policemen who were of Serbian origin continued to man that check-point on the bridge at Sanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM010, you're speaking very quickly. Could you please slow down so that your words will be translated and that we're not missing a word from your testimony. So try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question. I have a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may also ask a clarifying question, sir. At page 46, line 22, you're translated as having said: "They didn't sign that document." Now that sentence just comes out of the blue after you have been talking about the flag that was hoisted at the police station. Did you talk about a document that was not signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A relative of mine worked at the police. On the 25th of May, he was invited to come to the police station in Sanica, and he was asked to sign a document, to pledge loyalty in order to continue being a member of the police force. And since that document bore the symbol depicting four Ss, and -- and -- and it was a pledge to accept the situation as it was, i.e., that Muslims relinquished all of their rights, he didn't want to sign that document which was a loyalty pledge, and he was sent packing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, were both Serbs and Muslims free to pass by -- to move around the village and to pass by these check-points?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: No. From that moment on, from the 25th of May, the check-points at Sanica could be crossed only by women and children. Men were forbidden to move between the villages. It was strictly forbidden for the men to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether any differences would apply depending, based on the ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: Well, when I said that there were major differences between the two ethnicities, let me give you an example. Only a day after that, the workers who worked at the local Sanica factory, about 300 of them, on the 26th of May, were sent home. A certain number of villagers from my village were on a bus. When they arrived at the Sanica check-point, every single Muslim was taken off the buses, and they were said that they should proceed on foot. Only the Serbs were allowed to proceed on a bus, and the Muslims were told that they were not allowed to come back to work and not only to their workplace, but also to Sanica as a village, that their place was no longer in Sanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is only now that the translation has finished. So could I again urge you to slow down. I know it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, did you and the people you know feel safe in those days.

utterances.speaker: RM010
utterances.text: Of course, I could not feel safe. My movement was restricted. I was under surveillance 24 hours a day from a neighbouring hill. I did not even step out onto a road, which is 150 metres away from my house because I didn't feel safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
